Every attempt is listed on the card so you can audit the number. Results measure the path this phone is actually using right now, including any VPN or proxy that is switched on.

A network scanner that only reports what it actually measured. Every test is a real network operation - a real TCP connection, a real TLS handshake with certificate validation, a real DNS query, a real HTTP request. Nothing is simulated and no result is guessed. If a test could not be completed, the card says why instead of inventing a number.
The ms number - read this first

The big number on an IP result is the MEDIAN total time of the full HTTPS transaction: TCP connect + TLS handshake + HTTP request + first byte back, over all attempts. It is never the bare TCP connect time (that only measures one SYN round-trip to the nearest edge and flatters everything - it is shown separately as \'TCP median\'). With 4+ attempts the first run is dropped from the stats, because it pays cold costs (radio wake, route and TLS setup) and skews the result. Every attempt is printed on the card as \'total runs\' so you can audit the median yourself, and p90 shows the bad end of the spread. Jitter is the spread of those totals: high jitter = unstable path, whatever the median says.

Targets: one per line - single IPs, CIDR blocks (104.16.0.0/24), ranges (1.2.3.1-1.2.3.9), IPv6 for small ranges, or a whole file via 'Load from file'. 'Random Cloudflare IPs' draws addresses from Cloudflare's published ranges, and the hero card runs the classic one-tap scan: 100 random Cloudflare IPs over HTTPS with cloudflare.com as SNI.

Methods: TCP (bare connect - a reachability check, nothing more), HTTP (plain request on port 80), HTTPS (the real test: pinned to the IP, SNI + certificate checked for the hostname you set, then a real request), ICMP (system ping).

Hostname (SNI/Host): the name the TLS handshake is performed for. An IP only counts as a good Cloudflare IP if it answers correctly FOR that name.

Presets trade speed for certainty: more attempts and longer timeouts = slower but truer numbers. Workers is how many IPs are tested in parallel; very high parallelism on a weak connection distorts timings, which is why the accuracy defaults use 30.

Deep verify: after a scan, this re-tests the 10 best working IPs with 7 slower attempts and replaces their numbers - use it before trusting a winner.

Tap a card to copy the IP. The save button (star icon) saves it to the Vault. Export row copies/shares/saves the working list or the full list as plain text.

Reliability: success (every attempt worked), partial (most worked), unstable (some worked or jitter is high), failed. Score (0-100) blends success rate, median total time and jitter - it ranks, it does not grade truth.

Under each IP, the offline GeoIP line shows the country code in a small chip, then country, city and the owning network (AS number + organisation) from the databases bundled in the app - no internet needed and nothing leaves the phone.

Failures are classified honestly: timeout, refused, unreachable, TLS (handshake or certificate problem - the detail line says which), HTTP (connected but no valid HTTP answer).

Type the resolver IPs (or autofill a saved group, or the known-resolvers preset - global resolvers plus Iranian ones: Shecan, Electro, and 403.online which only answers from inside Iran), a test domain, a record type and a protocol. All resolvers are probed in parallel and each result appears as soon as its resolver answers. Your DNS settings are remembered between launches.

Record type AUTO picks for you: it asks for A first, and if the resolver answers but has no A records it tries AAAA - whichever produced addresses is what you see. Or pick one yourself: A, AAAA, MX, TXT, NS, CNAME, SOA, PTR, SRV.

Protocol AUTO also picks for you: plain UDP first, and where port 53 is intercepted or blocked it falls back to TCP, then DoT, then DoH for resolvers that publish a DoH host. The card shows the protocol that actually answered. Or force one: UDP/TCP - classic DNS on port 53. DoT - DNS over TLS on port 853. DoH - DNS over HTTPS; the query goes to the resolver IP with TLS for the DoH hostname.

IRAN OPTIMIZED (the card at the top of this tab) fills everything in for a filtered Iranian connection in one tap: Shecan, Electro and 403.online first (they answer from inside the country), Cloudflare and Google kept for comparison, Auto record type, Auto protocol, 5 attempts and a 4-second timeout for lossy mobile networks. The IP scanner has an 'Iran' preset chip with the same idea: fewer parallel workers so the scan itself does not congest your link, more attempts, longer timeout.

A resolver only counts as working when it returns a parseable DNS answer - an open port proves nothing. The headline number is the median answer time.

Poison warning: if every A/AAAA answer for a public name is a private/reserved address, the resolver is flagged as hijacked and excluded from 'working'. That is the signature of DNS interception: the name was redirected to a local block page or filter.

Give it a domain and it asks your phone's system DNS plus every known resolver for that domain's A and AAAA records - all in parallel, each row appearing as its resolver answers. If UDP is blocked for a resolver that supports DoH (Cloudflare, Google, Quad9, AdGuard), it retries over DoH and says so.

Badges: a green check means the answers match the majority. A warning triangle means this resolver's answers differ from what most resolvers said (stale, filtered, or a different CDN view), or that the resolver is poisoned (private IPs for a public name - shown in red). A cross means no answer at all.

Then every unique A-record IP is tested over HTTPS with the domain itself as SNI - so you see which of the domain's real IPs actually serve it from your connection, and can save the good ones to the Vault.

One tap, eight real checks on the connection you are using right now:

Snapshot - what Android reports: transport (Wi-Fi/mobile), private IP, gateway, DNS servers, whether a VPN is active, whether Android considers the internet validated.

Gateway - does your router answer ping. System DNS - a real query to the DNS your network assigned, with a poison check. Direct DNS 1.1.1.1 - the same query bypassing the assigned server; comparing the two exposes interception. HTTPS to 1.1.1.1 - pinned-IP HTTPS with SNI, end to end. IPv6 - whether an AAAA answer exists and TCP over IPv6 connects. Captive portal - the standard generate_204 check: anything but an empty 204 means a login page is intercepting. Exit identity - Cloudflare trace shows the exit IP, country, edge and WARP status the internet sees for you. Path MTU - the largest don't-fragment ping that gets through.

Your clean IPs, stored on the phone. Each entry remembers the SNI hostname it was verified with, so Retest always repeats the same test instead of a generic one. Add IPs from any result card (the save button with the star), or type them in with an optional label. Retest one or all; export the still-working ones or the whole list. The Vault is the answer to \'I found good IPs yesterday and lost them\'.

Named reusable lists. Create a group of IPs or of DNS resolvers in the Groups page (top bar, folder button), then autofill it into the IP scanner targets or the DNS scanner servers with one tap on its chip. \'Save as group\' under either scanner saves the current list under a name. Edit loads a group back into the editor; saving with the same name replaces it.
Every scan and diagnostics run is logged with its full results as plain text. Tap an entry to expand, copy or share it. History lives only on this phone and keeps the last 200 runs.

Language: English or Persian (full RTL, Vazirmatn font). Theme: dark or light. About shows whether the offline GeoIP databases loaded. ScanON has no accounts, no analytics and no server: scans go from your phone straight to the IPs and resolvers you test, and results never leave the device.

Anycast: a Cloudflare IP is not one machine; your request lands on a nearby edge, so timings say as much about your route as about the IP. VPN/proxy: if one is switched on, you are measuring through it - the Diagnostics snapshot tells you if a VPN is active. Mobile networks fluctuate minute to minute; a result is a measurement of that moment, which is why the Vault retest exists. And a fast HTTPS answer still does not guarantee an IP carries proxy traffic well under load - it is the strongest signal available without running the actual tunnel, and ScanON never pretends it is more than that.

Scans now live in the background of the app: switching tabs, rotating or opening History no longer kills a running scan, and a notification keeps long scans alive when you leave the app.

IP scanner: several ports at once (443, 2053, 8443...), a WebSocket check (WS: real RFC 6455 upgrade, only HTTP 101 counts), IPv6 CIDR of any size, random sampling of big ranges, packet-loss and jitter on every card, TLS version / cipher / certificate expiry, adaptive timeout, fail-fast, Rescan failed, Speed test (download through Cloudflare IPs), search, sort and latency filters, CSV and JSON export, progress with rate and ETA.

DNS: random query ids that are verified (spoofed answers rejected), EDNS0, automatic TCP retry for truncated answers, SERVFAIL/REFUSED no longer count as working, wider hijack detection (CGNAT, benchmark and other reserved ranges), HTTPS/CAA record types, IPv6 resolvers.

Data: one-file backup and restore of Vault, Groups, History and settings; Vault entries keep their port and show a trend of the last retests; history search, filters and undo.

Settings: system/dark/light theme, system/English/Persian language, reduce motion, haptics, keep screen on, compact layout.
Themes, accent, glass and density - applied instantly and remembered between launches.
How translucent the panels are and how strongly the background glows.
The dark/light choice applies to the Classic preset; the other presets have a fixed tone.

Settings, Appearance card. Five presets: Classic Teal (the 2.3/2.4 look, follows the dark/light choice), Obsidian Dark (carbon + electric cyan), Tokyo Night (indigo + neon magenta), Matrix Phosphor (monochrome emerald) and Frosted Daylight (alabaster + cobalt). Accent colour overrides the preset\'s primary colour. Glass intensity makes panels more translucent and the animated background glow stronger - lower it if your phone struggles. Density: Compact is the small 2.3 look, Comfortable is normal, Spacious adds room. Corner radius scales every card\'s corners. Result cards: tap copies the IP, the info button opens a details sheet with the full measurement (sparkline of every run, TLS, certificate, failures) and copy/save actions; the pulsing dot is the reliability at a glance.

New in 2.6. Tabs slide in from the side they sit on and settle with a spring; overlay pages (Settings, History, Groups, Guide) slide up instead. The cards on every screen cascade in one after another, result cards dip slightly when tapped, and the details section expands smoothly instead of snapping open. The scan progress bar is a gradient with a moving shimmer and an animated percentage, and the stat numbers count up to their values. The background gained a dot grid, a drifting aurora wash and a rotating radar sweep in the top corner, all in your theme colours, and the quick scan hero gradient slowly trades its two colours. If any of this feels heavy on your phone: Settings, Appearance, turn on Reduce motion or Static background and everything goes still while the app stays fast.
Motion in 2.7 - it reacts while you scan

New in 2.7. While any scan is running the whole background wakes up: fast pulse rings and a brighter wash fade in behind everything, and they fade back out when the scan ends. Result cards flash with your accent colour as they land, and every sparkline draws itself in from the left instead of appearing whole. The radar in the title bar turns slowly all the time, and faster in the progress card while a scan works. The Advanced section opens with a smooth expand instead of snapping, and the main scan buttons dip when pressed, like the result cards. Same escape hatch as before: Reduce motion in Settings, Appearance calms all of it down.

ScanON finds the IPs and DNS resolvers that actually work on your network - measured honestly, with full HTTPS and DNS transactions, never a bare ping dressed up as latency. Three quick choices and you are set.
Applies right away, the moment you pick it.
Pick a look now; every one of these can be changed later in Settings.
A few switches that shape the feel of the app. Change them any time in Settings.
Start a scan, then leave the app: the scan keeps running, a notification shows its progress, and you get told when it finishes. Your results are still here when you come back.

Tests resolvers the way DNS tunnel protocols really use them. The modes are protocols, not apps: Auto tests every carrier type at once (TXT, A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, SRV, NULL, HTTPS, SVCB, plus a long-name probe) and gives each resolver a verdict per protocol family. DNSTT also covers NoizDNS and Slipstream (same TXT wire format), MasterDNS covers the MasterDnsVPN, StormDNS and CottenDNS family, and Soar adds the long-name test it needs. Set your own tunnel zone as the test domain below - the app never fills a domain in for you. Each resolver is asked for A and TXT on your domain and for fresh random subdomains carrying the protocol data, which only your tunnel server can answer, so an intercepting resolver is exposed and a poisoned one never ranks. Ranking is by tunnel score: success rate first, then median, then jitter.

A tunnel scan tests whether resolvers can reach YOUR tunnel server, so without your tunnel domain as the test domain the results say nothing about any tunnel. Type your tunnel zone (the domain your tunnel is delegated on) into the test domain field first, or scan anyway and treat it as a plain resolver check.
Tap a provider to add its resolvers, or add every Iranian resolver we know at once. The 10.202.10.x services only answer from inside Iran.
Randomise the resolver order before scanning
When a working resolver is found, also test all 256 IPs in its /24 subnet
For every working resolver: a long-label query (like real tunnel traffic), a TXT query, and an outside lookup - proves the resolver can really carry a tunnel. Adds a few seconds per resolver.
CIDRs or IPs, one per line - every IP is tried as a resolver

New in 2.8. Scans no longer live on the screen you started them from: start an IP, DNS or domain scan, leave the app, even close it from recents - the scan keeps running under its progress notification and the results are waiting when you come back. Cancel still works from the scan card or from the app the notification opens. The vault retest-all works the same way.

Redesigned in 2.8.2. The tunnel card on the DNS tab works in protocols, not apps, because apps bundle protocols: SlipNet alone ships DNSTT, NoizDNS, VayDNS and Slipstream, and WhiteDNS is an app whose profiles run the MasterDNS family or Soar - there is no WhiteDNS protocol to scan for. Auto is the mode to use normally: it probes every carrier record type the protocols use (TXT, A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, SRV, NULL, HTTPS, SVCB) on fresh random subdomains of your test domain, adds a long-name probe, and prints a verdict per protocol family on each resolver card. The single-protocol modes test just that family: DNSTT (TXT both ways; NoizDNS and Slipstream share this wire format), VayDNS (TXT plus its alternate CNAME, A, AAAA, MX, NS and SRV carriers), MasterDNS (TXT, NULL, HTTPS, SVCB, MX - the odd types are the ones bad resolvers strip), Soar (TXT with its AAAA fallback, plus long names), TheFeed (TXT both ways). Your test domain is your own tunnel zone and is never filled in by the app; starting a tunnel scan without one warns you first, because resolvers can only be judged against the server they must actually reach. The tunnel score counts success rate first (loss is what kills a tunnel), then the full median, then jitter. Copy best pastes the winning resolver; the tunnel report lists the whole ranking. E2E verification stays the strictest check: a 48-character label query like real tunnel traffic, a TXT query, and an outside lookup through that resolver only.

Version 3.0 is about trusting the numbers. DNS ranking probes no longer ask the same question again and again - after the first answer, every attempt uses a fresh random subdomain, so each timed run is a real recursion instead of a cache hit (cache made mediocre resolvers look fast). Each ranked resolver also gets an honesty test: a name that cannot exist must return NXDOMAIN; a resolver that invents an address for it is flagged as hijacking and sorted below honest ones, and 0.0.0.0-style filter sinks count as poisoned. When a scan finishes, the top eight resolvers are quietly re-probed with extra attempts and their samples pooled, so the ranking you act on survived two rounds. Jitter is now the median absolute deviation, which one wild run cannot blow up. On the IP side, Quick Scan now fetches the Cloudflare /cdn-cgi/trace endpoint and only counts an IP when the reply really is a Cloudflare trace (a 200 with the right certificate was not proof enough - an interceptor can have both). The Iran card also grew: next to the resolver samples (now with a custom amount) it offers the /24 ranges those resolvers live in, loaded straight into the range field. And every field in the app now shows its label above the box instead of floating inside it.
SlipNet-style DNS options and more settings (2.8)

New in 2.8. The DNS scanner gained the options the SlipNet scanner has: a custom DNS port, UDP / TCP / Both transports, shuffle, nearby /24 expansion (a working resolver means its subnet is scanned too), a resolver list with Default, Import, country sets and custom ranges (every IP in a range is tried as a resolver), and E2E timeout and concurrency. It also gained speed presets (which since 2.8.3 show which one is active and confirm each tap). The Iran card changed in 2.8.3: the hand-picked provider list is gone, replaced by the net2share/ir-resolvers catalogue - thousands of resolver IPs that actually run inside Iranian datacenters - loaded as a random sample of 100, 250, 500, 1000 or all of them. The IP scanner gained a delay-between-attempts setting, Cloudflare port presets, and Iran fast, Iran deep and Battery saver speed presets. And the app now introduces itself on first run - language, theme and behaviour in three pages, shown once.
